sentence: At the tips hang about half a billion sacs.
claim: An adult's two lungs hold on average about 480 million alveoli (range 274–790 million in six lungs studied).
source_title: Ochs et al. 2004, The number of alveoli in the human lung, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 169:120 (PubMed)
note: Bible S18; excerpt: mean alveolar number 480 million (range 274–790 million; CV 37%). BioNumbers notes 480 million is for the pair of lungs. 'About half a billion' rounds 480 million (computed); the readout shows 480,000,000 with 'about'. Alveoli also line the respiratory bronchioles and ducts; 'at the tips' is the grape-cluster simplification.

sentence: Below your windpipe, the airways fork, again and again, up to about twenty-three times.
claim: In Weibel's classic model the airways branch dichotomously through about 23 generations from the trachea to the alveolar sacs.
source_title: Respiratory zone (Taylor & Francis Knowledge; Weibel's airway model)
note: Excerpt: 23 dichotomously branching airway generations comprising conducting and respiratory zones; some count 24 depending on whether the trachea is generation 0. A model of an average path; real branching is irregular. Review fix: 'up to about' (real paths run from about 8 to 25 generations).

sentence: Each is about a fifth of a millimetre.
claim: The mean volume of a single alveolus is about 4.2 million µm³, a diameter of about 0.2 mm.
source_title: Ochs et al. 2004, The number of alveoli in the human lung, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 169:120 (PubMed)
note: Excerpt: the mean size of a single alveolus was rather constant at 4.2 × 10⁶ µm³. Computed: a sphere of that volume has a diameter (6V/π)^(1/3) ≈ 200 µm = a fifth of a millimetre. Alveoli are not spheres; 'about'.

sentence: For centuries, physicians taught the lung was airy flesh, there to cool the heart.
claim: In the Galenic tradition the lungs were thought to be fleshy (made of coagulated blood), and their function was held to be cooling the heart; Malpighi overturned both views.
source_title: Malpighi, Marcello (Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography, Encyclopedia.com)
note: Excerpts: in Galenic medicine the lungs were considered to be made up of coagulated blood; Malpighi held that the lungs did not cool the heart, 'as had previously been supposed'. 'Physicians' is the plain reading of the tradition he overturned. Review fix: 'airy flesh', not 'fleshy': Galen described the lung's tissue as light and foam-like; the shot is an illustration, not a solid lung.

sentence: In sixteen sixty-one, Marcello Malpighi put a frog's lung under a microscope: bubbles.
claim: In 1661, in De pulmonibus (letters to Borelli), Malpighi showed with a microscope that the lungs have a vesicular (bubble-like) structure, not a fleshy one, and described the capillaries in frog lungs.
source_title: Malpighi, Marcello (Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography, Encyclopedia.com)
note: Excerpt: using a microscope he showed that the lungs had a vesicular structure rather than being fleshy; the trachea's branches end in the vesicles; in the second letter, frog lungs, he described the capillaries. 'Bubbles' = vesicles (alveoli). Review fix: he worked mainly on frog lungs (the excerpt's second letter), hence 'a frog's lung'.

sentence: Each sac is wrapped in capillaries.
claim: The alveoli are surrounded by a dense network of capillaries where gas exchange takes place.
source_title: 22.4: Gas Exchange and Transport (JoVE Science Education, following OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 22.4)
note: Excerpt (JoVE 22.4): alveoli and capillaries are intertwined and physically touch; both one cell thick, so gas exchange occurs easily. (Malpighi described the capillaries, c5.)

sentence: At its thinnest, the wall between air and blood is about half a micrometre: far thinner than a red cell.
claim: The blood–air barrier is about 0.3–0.5 µm thick (averaging about 0.6 µm in some measurements), against a red cell about 7.5 µm across (episode 1).
source_title: Physiology, Lung (StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf NBK493219; bible S19)
note: Bible S19; excerpts: barrier 0.3–0.5 µm; a physiology lecture gives an average about 0.6 µm, as thin as 0.2 µm. 'About half a micrometre' sits in that span. A red cell is 7–8 µm across (episode 1, c2): over ten times wider (computed). Review fix: 'at its thinnest' (Weibel's harmonic-mean thickness is about 0.6 µm, the arithmetic mean about 2 µm).

sentence: Oxygen slips across, no pump needed.
claim: Oxygen moves from the alveolar air into the blood by passive diffusion, down its partial-pressure gradient; no active transport is involved.
source_title: 22.4: Gas Exchange and Transport (JoVE Science Education, following OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 22.4)
note: Excerpt (JoVE 22.4): gas travels from areas of higher partial pressure to lower; oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood. 'Drifts' = diffuses (passive; no pump).

sentence: Thicken that wall, and breathing gets harder.
claim: When the alveolar walls thicken and scar (as in pulmonary fibrosis), oxygen crosses into the blood less easily and people typically become short of breath, at first on exertion.
source_title: Frontiers for Young Minds, 2021 (Core Concept: Human Health), on pulmonary fibrosis
note: Excerpts: gas exchange works best when the alveoli are thin; with fibrosis less oxygen gets into the body with every breath. A review (PMC4422352, Am J Physiol) describes a stiff lung with compromised gas exchange and shortness of breath on exertion. Stated as a mechanism, no advice; the disease is not named on air.

sentence: Unfold every sac flat, and they'd cover at least seventy square metres.
claim: The alveolar (gas-exchange) surface of adult lungs is about 70–100 m²; morphometric estimates run to 120–140 m².
source_title: Physiology, Lung (StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf NBK493219; bible S19)
note: Bible S19 (70–100 m²) and S20 (120–140 m² by morphometry). 'About seventy' is the low, commonly cited figure (a lecture: about 70 m² in a healthy adult male). The readout says about 70 m². Review fix: 'at least', since morphometric figures run to about 130 m².

sentence: At least a third of a tennis court, folded inside your chest.
claim: A singles tennis court is 23.77 m × 8.23 m = 195.6 m² (ITF); 70 m² is about 36% of it.
source_title: Tennis court (Wikipedia, citing the ITF Rules of Tennis)
note: Excerpt: 78 ft (23.77 m) long, 27 ft (8.23 m) wide for singles (ITF Rules of Tennis). Computed: 23.77 × 8.23 = 195.6 m²; 70 / 195.6 = 0.36, 'about a third'. (At 100 m² it is about half: the comparison is for the 70 m² figure said.) Review fix: 'at least a third' (it holds for 70 m² and grows with the larger estimates); the whoa's shot draws the court's lines.

claim: Inhaled air does not go into a single hollow bag: the lung's inside is divided into hundreds of millions of alveoli.
source_title: Malpighi, Marcello (Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography, Encyclopedia.com)
note: As c1 and c5: vesicular, not hollow and not fleshy. 'Balloons' is the common picture the takeaway corrects.

sentence: So your lungs aren't a bag.
claim: Inhaled air does not go into a single hollow bag: the lung's inside is divided into hundreds of millions of alveoli.
source_title: Malpighi, Marcello (Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography, Encyclopedia.com)
note: As c1 and c5: vesicular, not hollow and not fleshy. 'Balloons' is the common picture the takeaway corrects.

sentence: They're a sponge that spreads air thin.
claim: The branching airways and alveoli spread the inhaled air over a very large, very thin surface for diffusion.
source_title: 22.4: Gas Exchange and Transport (JoVE Science Education, following OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 22.4)
note: As c6–c9: the large area (c9) and thin barrier (c7) are what make diffusion fast enough. 'Sponge' is a metaphor for the alveolar structure.

claim: At rest an adult moves roughly 5–8 L of air a minute (about 500 mL a breath, 12–20 breaths a minute); the tally uses 6 L a minute.
source_title: Physiology, Tidal Volume (StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf NBK482502)
note: Excerpts: StatPearls tidal volume about 500 mL (male), about 400 mL (female); American Lung Association 12–20 breaths a minute; JoVE gives 5–8 L/min at rest. Review fix: the tally runs at 6 L/min, a common resting figure; the line lands near 62 s, about 6.2 L (computed): 'about six'.

claim: White blood cells leave the bloodstream by rolling along, arresting on and crawling over the vessel lining, then migrating through the vessel wall (transmigration).
source_title: Ley et al. 2007, Getting to the site of inflammation: the leukocyte adhesion cascade updated, Nat Rev Immunol (PubMed; bible S22)
note: Bible S22: rolling, arrest, crawling, then migration through the wall. Episode 6 tells it.
